title: Live in Chicago: How Public Relations Works
summary: Live recording at the Athenaeum Theatre in Chicago, in which Josh and Chuck explore public relations through the career of Edward Bernays, often called the father of public relations. They cover his debt to his uncle Sigmund Freud and the idea of the unconscious self, the shift from straightforward advertising to desire-based ads, and his campaigns for Lucky Strike (Torches of Freedom), Beech-Nut bacon, Vaniteee hairnets (Nita/Vanity Fair-style hairnet work, as named in the episode), and the Bananas/United Fruit work that fed into the 1954 Guatemala coup. They discuss his book Propaganda, the term "public relations," the "nudge" politics idea, and close with a list of PR disasters: US Airways, Philip Morris Czech study, Abercrombie & Fitch, Coca-Cola Magic Can, Strongbow cider, and Domino's Noid and the 2009 Atlanta hostage standoff.

segments.title: Live opening and setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck welcome the live Chicago audience at the Athenaeum Theatre, joke about Jerry's absence, sample a Chicago drink, and tease the topic of public relations and Edward Bernays.

segments.title: Definition of PR and Edward Bernays
segments.summary: They read the Bureau of Labor Statistics definition of PR specialists, then introduce Edward Bernays as the man who created the public relations job and call him one of the most influential and most evil people of the twentieth century. They mention Life magazine's ranking and his long career.

segments.title: Freud, the unconscious self, and advertising shift
segments.summary: Bernays borrowed from his uncle Sigmund Freud's ideas about unconscious desires and herd mentality to manipulate consumers. Advertising moved from straightforward product explanations to appeals to fear and desire, and planned obsolescence grew after World War One and World War Two.

segments.title: Bernays' clients and Goebbels' admiration
segments.summary: They list Bernays' clients, including Thomas Edison, Henry Ford, and Eleanor Roosevelt, and the unverified claim that Hitler wanted to hire him. They mention the documentary Century of the Self and that Goebbels admired Bernays' work. They describe early tactics such as expert endorsements and product placement, and the Hearst magazine and diamond ads with Clara Bow.

segments.title: Bernays' early life, family, and Damaged Goods
segments.summary: Bernays was born in Vienna in 1891 to parents who were siblings-in-law of Freud. After Cornell, he worked on promoting the play Damaged Goods about syphilis, using a campaign that got the subject into national conversation and sold tickets.

segments.title: Propaganda book and the term public relations
segments.summary: Bernays' first book, Crystallizing Public Opinion, was sent to Freud, who responded with a lukewarm letter. Freud later had money trouble, and Bernays helped publish his work in America. Bernays' second book was Propaganda, and he chose the term public relations because propaganda had a bad reputation after Nazi use.

segments.title: Bernays' views on the public and elite manipulation
segments.summary: The hosts describe Bernays' hierarchical view that the public needs a select few to guide it and that choices should be narrowed. They discuss his use of special pleaders and how his clients disliked him but valued his results.

segments.title: Vanity hairnet campaign
segments.summary: Bernays was hired by a hairnet company after bobbed hair reduced demand. He enlisted artists to praise hairnets and had manufacturers and factories promote them for safety, which boosted sales.

segments.title: Torches of Freedom and women smoking
segments.summary: For American Tobacco and George Washington Hill, Bernays staged the Torches of Freedom in the 1929 Easter Parade in New York, with debutantes lighting cigarettes to frame smoking as women's liberation. Nurse Florence Lindon taught women etiquette about smoking, and Bernays made Lucky Strike green fashionable.

segments.title: Bacon as a breakfast food
segments.summary: Bernays was hired by Beech-Nut to promote bacon for breakfast. He used doctors' endorsements and a study that supported a hearty breakfast with bacon, which helped establish bacon as a breakfast food.

segments.title: United Fruit, bananas, and Guatemala
segments.summary: The hosts trace United Fruit from Lorenzo Dow Baker's banana trade in Jamaica in 1870 to its control of Central American economies. Bernays promoted bananas through the Middle America Information Bureau. When Guatemalan president Jacobo Arbenz pushed land reform, United Fruit worked with Bernays and the CIA on a Red Scare campaign and the 1954 coup that started a long civil war.

segments.title: Nudge politics and legacy
segments.summary: The hosts connect Bernays' ideas to nudge politics, a 2008 idea adopted as government policy under a presidential executive order. They discuss how nudges can become shoves when the decision-makers are not trustworthy.

segments.title: Bernays' death and remarks
segments.summary: They note Bernays was interviewed at age one hundred and stood by his work. They say he died at 103 and his last words were that he had said people were stupid.

segments.title: PR disasters: US Airways, Philip Morris, Abercrombie & Fitch
segments.summary: The hosts begin a list of PR disasters: a US Airways customer feedback link that led to a pornographic image, Philip Morris's Czech study claiming smoking saved money, and Abercrombie & Fitch's racist Wong Brothers Laundry shirt and thong line for young girls.

segments.title: Coca-Cola Magic Can and Strongbow cider
segments.summary: Coca-Cola's early 1990s Magic Can promotion, with a prize that shot out, led to people drinking the chlorinated water inside and poison lines getting calls, forcing ads warning people not to drink it. Strongbow cider used a photo of anti-alcohol campaigner Hugh Price Hughes as its founder.

segments.title: Domino's Noid and Atlanta hostage standoff
segments.summary: A man named Kenneth Lamar Ennis stormed a Domino's in Atlanta in January 2009 with a gun, held employees hostage, and was later sentenced to a psychiatric facility after believing Domino's targeted him with the Noid ads. He later died by suicide. Domino's then launched a Facebook game in 2011.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank the Chicago audience and close the show.
